title: Water Quality
text: How land use and policy affect Florida’s springs, rivers, and groundwater, and how planning can protect them.

title: Water Quality
section: A Short History of Water Quality
text:
A Short History of Water Quality
Water quality science began with tracing disease and grew into regulating everything from factory pipes to farm runoff.

Show the timelineHide the timeline 11 moments, 1854–2024

  Foundations
  1854The Broad Street pumpJohn Snow maps cholera deaths in London and traces them to a contaminated well, an early landmark of public health and spatial analysis.
  1908Chlorinated drinking waterJersey City becomes the first U.S. city to disinfect its public water supply continuously with chlorine.
  Federal regulation
  1969The Cuyahoga River fireA burning river in Ohio becomes a national symbol of water pollution.
  1972Clean Water ActCongress requires permits for pollution discharged from pipes and sets the goal of fishable, swimmable waters.
  1974Safe Drinking Water ActEPA gets the authority to set national standards for public drinking water.
  1987Nonpoint source pollutionAmendments to the Clean Water Act add a program for runoff from farms, lawns, and streets, now the leading cause of impaired waters.
  1993The biosolids ruleEPA's Part 503 rule sets national standards for applying treated sewage sludge to land.
  New challenges
  1998Nutrient pollutionStephen Carpenter and colleagues show how nitrogen and phosphorus runoff drive algae blooms in lakes and rivers.
  2014Flint and ToledoLead contamination in Flint and an algae toxin in Toledo's water supply show how drinking water failures fall hardest on some communities.
  2023Sackett v. EPAThe Supreme Court narrows which wetlands the Clean Water Act protects.
  2024PFAS limitsEPA sets the first national drinking water limits for PFAS "forever chemicals." In 2025 it moves to roll back some of them.

title: Water Quality
text:
In Florida
Florida sits on porous limestone, so what happens on the land can reach springs, rivers, and the aquifer most residents drink from. That makes land-use planning a water-quality decision.

  1947Everglades National ParkThe park is established to protect part of the River of Grass.
  1994Everglades Forever ActFlorida sets phosphorus limits and builds treatment marshes to clean water flowing into the Everglades.
  1999Watershed Restoration ActFlorida begins setting pollution limits for impaired waters and later adopts basin plans, including one for Lake Okeechobee.
  2000Comprehensive Everglades Restoration PlanThe state and federal governments launch a decades-long plan to restore water flow through South Florida.
  2016Springs and Aquifer Protection ActOutstanding Florida Springs get recovery plans to reduce pollution and over-pumping.
  2021New biosolids ruleFlorida's updated biosolids rule takes effect, aimed at keeping phosphorus from biosolids out of waterways.

title: Water Quality
text:
Key Readings

Carpenter, S. R., et al. (1998). Nonpoint pollution of surface waters with phosphorus and nitrogen. Ecological Applications, 8(3), 559–568.
Grunwald, M. (2006). The Swamp: The Everglades, Florida, and the Politics of Paradise. Simon & Schuster.
Karr, J. R., & Dudley, D. R. (1981). Ecological perspective on water quality goals. Environmental Management, 5(1), 55–68.
Snow, J. (1855). On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (2nd ed.). John Churchill.

title: Sustainability
text: How planning choices about growth, land, and resources shape whether Florida stays livable, and what it takes to plan for the long term.

title: Sustainability
text:
A Short History of Sustainability
Sustainability started as a rule for managing forests and grew into one of the central ideas in planning. These are the moments that shaped how the field thinks about it today.

Show the timelineHide the timeline 17 moments, 1713–2017

  Roots
  1713Sustained yieldHans Carl von Carlowitz, a German mining official, argues forests should only be cut as fast as they regrow. His word, nachhaltig, is the origin of "sustainable."
  1798Limits of resourcesThomas Malthus warns that population can outpace food supply, starting a long debate about growth and natural limits.
  1864Man and NatureGeorge Perkins Marsh shows how human activity degrades land and water, one of the first systematic accounts of environmental damage.
  1949The land ethicAldo Leopold's A Sand County Almanac argues people are members of a land community, not just its users.

  Environmental awakening
  1962Silent SpringRachel Carson documents the effects of pesticides, helping launch the modern environmental movement.
  1968Tragedy of the commonsGarrett Hardin argues shared resources get overused when individuals act in their own interest.
  1969Design with NatureIan McHarg layers maps of soils, water, and habitat to decide where development fits. It's a direct ancestor of GIS-based planning.
  1972The Limits to GrowthA computer-modeling study for the Club of Rome projects that unchecked growth will hit planetary limits. The UN holds its first environment conference in Stockholm the same year.

  Sustainable development
  1987The Brundtland definitionThe UN report Our Common Future defines sustainable development as meeting present needs "without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs."
  1990Governing the commonsElinor Ostrom shows communities can manage shared resources well without privatization or top-down control. She later wins the 2009 Nobel Prize in Economics.
  1992Rio Earth SummitNations adopt Agenda 21, which pushes sustainability down to local governments and planning.
  1994Triple bottom lineJohn Elkington frames sustainability as balancing economic, social, and environmental outcomes.

  Planning and justice
  1996The planner's triangleScott Campbell's "Green Cities, Growing Cities, Just Cities?" shows planners are caught between economic growth, environmental protection, and social equity, and that these goals often conflict.
  2003Just sustainabilitiesJulian Agyeman, Robert Bullard, and Bob Evans argue sustainability can't be separated from equity and environmental justice.

  Today
  2009Planetary boundariesJohan Rockström and colleagues identify nine Earth systems, from climate to nitrogen cycles, with limits humanity shouldn't cross.
  2015Sustainable Development GoalsThe UN adopts 17 goals for 2030, including clean water, sustainable cities, and reduced inequality.
  2017Doughnut economicsKate Raworth pictures a safe zone between meeting everyone's basic needs and staying within planetary limits.

title: Sustainability
text:
In Florida
Florida keeps growing, and every new neighborhood, road, and treatment plant commits land and resources for decades. Sustainability in planning means weighing those long-term costs before they’re locked in.

  1972Areas of Critical State ConcernThe Environmental Land and Water Management Act lets the state protect places like the Florida Keys and Big Cypress from harmful development.
  1985Growth Management ActEvery city and county must adopt a comprehensive plan, with state review and a requirement that infrastructure keep pace with growth.
  2011Community Planning ActThe state scales back its oversight of local plans and eliminates the Department of Community Affairs, shifting more control to local governments.
  2016Springs and Aquifer Protection ActFlorida designates Outstanding Florida Springs and requires recovery plans for springs harmed by pollution and over-pumping.

text:
Key Readings

Agyeman, J., Bullard, R. D., & Evans, B. (Eds.). (2003). Just Sustainabilities: Development in an Unequal World. MIT Press.
Campbell, S. (1996). Green cities, growing cities, just cities? Urban planning and the contradictions of sustainable development. Journal of the American Planning Association, 62(3), 296–312.
McHarg, I. L. (1969). Design with Nature. Natural History Press.
Meadows, D. H., Meadows, D. L., Randers, J., & Behrens, W. W. (1972). The Limits to Growth. Universe Books.
Ostrom, E. (1990). Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action. Cambridge University Press.
Rockström, J., et al. (2009). A safe operating space for humanity. Nature, 461, 472–475.

title: Why I’m putting my research out in the open
text:
Most research ends up in a journal article or a conference talk that a few hundred people see. But the questions I work on, like how growth reaches rural counties, who lives with environmental burdens, and what’s happening to Florida’s water, belong to everyone who lives here.
So this is where I’ll share the work as it happens.
What to expect:

Maps with plain-language notes
Explainers on Florida planning
Research updates
Reading picks from the news and journals

If you want somewhere to start, try the maps.

title: Interdisciplinary & Transdisciplinary Research
text:
Environmental problems cut across fields. I draw on the social sciences to understand people, policy, and power, and on the quantitative sciences to measure what’s happening on the ground.
Transdisciplinary work goes one step further, bringing in the knowledge of communities, agencies, and practitioners outside academia so the research answers questions people in Florida are actually asking.

title: Interdisciplinary & Transdisciplinary Research
section: A Short History of Interdisciplinary & Transdisciplinary Research
text:
A Short History of Interdisciplinary & Transdisciplinary Research
Working across fields is an old idea, but it took off as researchers faced problems no single discipline could solve.

Show the timelineHide the timeline 9 moments, 1959–2012

  Two cultures
  1959The Two CulturesC. P. Snow warns that the sciences and humanities have stopped talking to each other.
  1970Transdisciplinarity is namedJean Piaget uses the term at an OECD seminar on interdisciplinary teaching and research.
  Problems that cross boundaries
  1973Wicked problemsHorst Rittel and Melvin Webber argue planning problems have no single right answer and can't be solved by one discipline.
  1984Complexity scienceThe Santa Fe Institute is founded to study complex systems across physics, biology, economics, and social science.
  1994Mode 2 knowledgeMichael Gibbons and colleagues describe research that is organized around real-world problems instead of disciplines.
  Science with society
  2001Sustainability scienceRobert Kates and colleagues call for a new field linking nature and society to support sustainable development.
  2004Facilitating Interdisciplinary ResearchThe U.S. National Academies recommend ways for universities and funders to support work across fields.
  2009Social-ecological systemsElinor Ostrom publishes a framework for studying how people and ecosystems shape each other.
  2012Transdisciplinary practiceDaniel Lang and colleagues set out principles for research that includes communities and practitioners from the start.

title: Environmental Justice
text: Who ends up living with environmental burdens, how those patterns form, and who gets a voice in the decisions behind them.

title: Environmental Justice
section: A Short History of Environmental Justice
text:
A Short History of Environmental Justice
Environmental justice grew out of Black-led community protests in the 1980s. Ever since, its central questions have been how race and class shape who lives with pollution and who gets a say.

Show the timelineHide the timeline 14 moments, 1979–2025

  Roots of the movement
  1979Bean v. Southwestern WasteHouston residents use civil rights law to challenge the siting of a landfill in their neighborhood, one of the first lawsuits of its kind.
  1982Warren County protestsResidents of a majority-Black county in North Carolina protest a PCB landfill, and hundreds are arrested. It's often called the birth of the movement.
  1983The GAO landfill studyA federal study finds three of four hazardous waste landfills in the Southeast are in majority-Black communities.
  1987Toxic Wastes and RaceA national study by the United Church of Christ finds race is the strongest predictor of where hazardous waste facilities are located.
  Building a field
  1990Dumping in DixieRobert Bullard documents how Black communities in the South bear the burden of polluting facilities, laying the groundwork for EJ research.
  1991Principles of Environmental JusticeThe First National People of Color Environmental Leadership Summit adopts 17 principles that still guide the movement.
  1994Executive Order 12898Federal agencies are directed to address disproportionate environmental impacts on minority and low-income communities.
  Race, class, or both?
  1994Which came first?Vicki Been asks whether polluting facilities are sited in poor communities of color, or whether housing markets push lower-income residents toward them after they're built. The race-versus-class debate shapes the field for decades.
  2007Toxic Wastes and Race at TwentyBullard, Mohai, Saha, and Wright update the 1987 study with better methods and find racial disparities are even larger than first reported, even after accounting for income.
  2007Three dimensions of justiceDavid Schlosberg's Defining Environmental Justice separates distribution (who bears burdens), recognition (whose concerns count), and participation (who decides).
  2014Toxic CommunitiesDorceta Taylor shows how residential segregation, housing discrimination, and land markets concentrate pollution in communities of color.
  2016Beyond the cityRural scholars show the same patterns of race and class play out in rural places too. More on the Urban–Rural Planning page.
  Today
  2021Justice40A federal initiative aims to direct 40% of the benefits of certain federal investments to disadvantaged communities.
  2025Federal rollbackA new executive order revokes Executive Order 12898 and other federal environmental justice orders.

title: Environmental Justice
text:
In Florida
In Florida, the costs of growth and waste don’t land evenly. Some communities, often Black, Latino, or lower-income, end up hosting the facilities and land uses that others avoid, with less say in how those decisions get made.

  1968Overtown and I-95Interstate 95 is routed through Overtown, the historic heart of Black Miami. Its construction directly displaces about 8,500 households.
  1996"Mount Dioxin," PensacolaAfter years of organizing by Citizens Against Toxic Exposure, Black residents living beside the Escambia Wood Treating Superfund site win relocation for 358 households.
  2018Climate gentrificationA Harvard study finds homes on higher ground in Miami-Dade gaining value faster than low-lying ones, raising concern that rising costs will push lower-income residents out of neighborhoods like Little Haiti.

title: Environmental Justice
text:
Key Readings

Been, V. (1994). Locally undesirable land uses in minority neighborhoods: Disproportionate siting or market dynamics? Yale Law Journal, 103(6), 1383–1422.
Bullard, R. D. (1990). Dumping in Dixie: Race, Class, and Environmental Quality. Westview Press.
Bullard, R. D., Mohai, P., Saha, R., & Wright, B. (2007). Toxic Wastes and Race at Twenty: 1987–2007. United Church of Christ Justice and Witness Ministries.
Commission for Racial Justice, United Church of Christ. (1987). Toxic Wastes and Race in the United States.
Fernandez, E. (2026). Urban-rural transfer and distributive environmental justice in biosolids land application: A geographic information systems (GIS) analysis of Florida. Journal of Rural Studies, 126, 104324.
Schlosberg, D. (2007). Defining Environmental Justice: Theories, Movements, and Nature. Oxford University Press.
Keenan, J. M., Hill, T., & Gumber, A. (2018). Climate gentrification: From theory to empiricism in Miami-Dade County, Florida. Environmental Research Letters, 13(5), 054001.
Taylor, D. E. (2014). Toxic Communities: Environmental Racism, Industrial Pollution, and Residential Mobility. NYU Press.

title: Dissertation
text: My dissertation examines how planning processes and policy framing shape biosolids governance in Florida, with a focus on urban–rural distribution and environmental justice. It traces how biosolids policies are developed, implemented, and contested across multiple scales of governance, and links planning theory and environmental justice to regional waste management.

title: Dissertation
text:
Biosolids in Florida

Biosolids are the treated solids left over from wastewater treatment. In Florida, much of this material is spread on land as fertilizer, often far from the cities that produce it. That raises questions about water quality, rural communities, and who decides.

Biosolids in Florida: An Assessment of Management and Impacts
1000 Friends of Florida, 2025. My role: GIS analysis, spatial assessment, policy analysis, and co-authorship.

Florida’s Impaired Waters
Florida checks the health of its rivers, lakes, springs, estuaries, and coastal waters by dividing them into assessment units called waterbody IDs (WBIDs). Waters that fail state standards for things like nutrients, bacteria, or dissolved oxygen go on the verified impaired list, which means the state has to set a pollution limit for them. title: Urban–Rural Planning
text: Rural places often absorb the costs of urban growth. I study how state and local policy plays out across the urban–rural divide.

title: Urban–Rural Planning
section: A Short History of Urban–Rural Planning
text:
A Short History of Urban–Rural Planning
Planners have argued for more than a century about how cities and the countryside depend on each other. The divide has always been blurrier than the maps suggest.

Show the timelineHide the timeline 13 moments, 1898–2024

  Early ideas
  1898The town-country magnetEbenezer Howard's garden city idea tries to combine the best of city and countryside in one planned community.
  1915The city-regionPatrick Geddes's Cities in Evolution treats a city and its surrounding region as one connected system.
  1923Regional planning in the U.S.Lewis Mumford, Benton MacKaye, and others form the Regional Planning Association of America to plan whole regions, not just cities.
  1933Tennessee Valley AuthorityThe federal government takes on large-scale regional planning in the rural South, from dams to electricity to land management.
  Growth at the edge
  1956Interstate highwaysThe Federal-Aid Highway Act speeds suburban and exurban growth into farmland at the urban fringe.
  1981Farmland Protection Policy ActFederal projects must consider how they convert farmland to other uses.
  Rethinking the divide
  1998Rural-urban interactionsCecilia Tacoli argues flows of people, goods, money, and waste between city and country matter more than the line between them.
  2011Rural America in an urban societyDaniel Lichter and David Brown show how rural places are tied into urban economies, labor markets, and politics.
  2014Planetary urbanizationNeil Brenner and Christian Schmid argue urbanization reshapes even remote landscapes through mines, farms, and infrastructure.
  Rural environmental justice
  2016Urban-rural exploitationKelly-Reif and Wing name the pattern of cities exporting burdens like waste, pollution, and industrial farming to rural communities.
  2016Rural voices in EJDavid Pellow calls on environmental justice and rural studies scholars to work together, and Ashwood and MacTavish show how rural residents get outvoted on decisions that put burdens in their communities.
  2019Urban-Rural LinkagesUN-Habitat publishes guiding principles for planning cities and rural areas together.
  2024Landscapes in transitionBrown and colleagues show how climate-driven landscape changes in Europe, from energy projects to conservation, create new rural justice conflicts.

title: Urban–Rural Planning
text:
In Florida
Florida’s cities depend on rural land for food, water, and space for what cities produce, from farmland to waste. Rural counties often have fewer planning resources to shape how that relationship works.

  1979Right to Farm ActFlorida protects farm operations from nuisance claims. Later amendments bar local governments from restricting farm activities covered by state best management practices.
  1985Growth Management ActEvery city and county must adopt a comprehensive plan, including how rural land is used.
  1999Florida ForeverThe state launches a land conservation program that buys and protects natural and rural lands.
  2011Community Planning ActState review of local plans is scaled back, leaving rural counties with fewer planning resources to manage growth pressure.
  2026Biosolids flowsMy research traces how biosolids produced in Florida's metro counties are applied in less populated rural counties.
